Mubarak is the managing director and group CEO of Mubadala, a $330bn sovereign wealth fund whose main shareholder is the Abu Dhabi government.
Mubarak has chaired City since 2008. In 2013, he received a Commander of the Order of the British Empire honour, partly for strengthening cultural ties between the UK and the UAE, including through the football club’s acquisition.
The investigation found that City’s owners had “concealed the true state of its finances from its auditors and football regulators” to bypass spending limits between 2008 and 2018.
City have denied the charges, rejected the findings and said they would appeal. There is no suggestion that Mubarak has engaged in wrongdoing.
The club used "sham" commercial contracts to artificially inflate revenues and reduce costs by more than $1bn, the findings showed.
"The Club’s financial statements had not been prepared and audited in accordance with applicable legal and regulatory principles," the commission wrote.
It was "reckless" and "acted other than with utmost good faith", it added.

By contrast, Avengers: Endgame Encore, an extended re-release of the 2019 Marvel film, managed only €356,000 ($404,000) during the same period in Italy.

The documentary features interviews with 24 Israeli military and intelligence insiders, whose identities remained anonymous.
NAZA drew a record-breaking 24-and-a-half-minute standing ovation at its world premiere, the longest at Venice, according to Variety.
The reception surpassed the 22-minute ovation given last year to Kaouther Ben Hania’s The Voice of Hind Rajab , which tells the story of the five-year-old Palestinian girl killed by Israeli forces in Gaza in January 2024.

On 28 September, residents of Erbil heard military aircraft overhead as the US‑led coalition against the Islamic State group (IS) was preparing for its full withdrawal.
That same night, three Iranian drones hit a camp belonging to an Iranian Kurdish opposition party in Koya. Two days later, Koya was hit again by a drone, the first such attack after the coalition’s departure.
On Wednesday, the US‑led coalition ended its more than decade‑long mission in Iraq, a mission that began in 2014 when IS seized large territories in Iraq and Syria and carried out mass atrocities.
Although the militant group was declared defeated in Iraq in 2017 and in Syria in 2019, coalition forces remained to help contain its remnants.
In 2024, Baghdad and Washington agreed to wind down the mission, prompting a gradual withdrawal from bases across Iraq and a final consolidation in the Kurdistan Region before the complete pullout, scheduled for 30 September.
The latest incidents in Koya underscore how exposed the Iraqi Kurdistan Region remains to drone and missile attacks amid ongoing tensions between Iran and the United States.

The strike hit a cart attached to a minibus used to transport passengers amid severe fuel shortages and soaring transport costs across the enclave.
Such vehicles are often packed with dozens of people travelling between different areas of the Strip.
“The Israeli missile struck the civilian transport vehicle at a crowded hour of the day, when the streets were full of displaced people moving around,” Motaz Ayoub, a civil defence ambulance officer who was among the first responders to reach the scene, told Middle East Eye.
“When we arrived, many of the killed and wounded were scattered across the street. We did not know who they were or where they had come from. One man's body was cut off, and many of the injured were in critical condition.”
Ayoub said a bus passing close to the vehicle was also hit, leaving several passengers wounded.
Ayman Shubair, 47, was inside his mobile phone shop about 100 metres from the site of the strike.

On
Benjamin Netanyahu’s whirlwind visit to the United States last week to address the United Nations General Assembly was further evidence that the Israeli prime minister is now a universal pariah.
He is being abandoned even by his closest allies.
It was perhaps not surprising that 77 nations, including a handful of European states, walked out of the chamber in protest that a wanted war crimes suspect - a fugitive from the International Criminal Court (ICC) - was being given a platform to speak on the world’s largest stage.
Far more notable was what happened - or rather, didn’t - away from the podium. Netanyahu spent just eight hours in the US before heading back to Israel. It is hard to believe that that was his choice.
He was denied his usual moment in the sun with Donald Trump at the White House, and could not even secure a meeting with Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
There was no invitation to address the US Congress, and with it familiar scenes of legislators rapturously celebrating his anti-Palestinian incitement.
Israel's former ambassador to Washington, Michael Oren, told Reuters: "I don't recall a time when the prime minister came to the United States and didn't meet with the president.”
The shunning of Netanyahu stood in stark contrast to the reception of Xi Jinping. The Chinese leader was personally greeted at the airport by Trump with a red carpet and military flyover.

A rapid offensive by Yemen’s Houthis has intensified the country’s civil war and caused chaos in global oil markets.
The group, which has controlled much of northern Yemen for over a decade, has seized fresh territory from the pro-government forces and threatened shipping traffic, notably that of Saudi Arabia, in the Bab el-Mandeb strait, the maritime chokepoint linking the Gulf of Aden to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal.
With few signs of military formality, the group has often been described in international media as a "ragtag fighting force".
But over the past two decades, the Houthis have evolved to use missiles and drones to stage attacks inside Yemen as well as against Israel, Saudi Arabia and the UAE, among others.
Much of the group’s arsenal has either been designed or supplied by Iran, which regards the force as a member of its Axis of Resistance, a network of allies that also includes Hamas and Hezbollah.
The Houthis have also acquired weapons, including decades-old Soviet-era tanks and helicopters, after victory on the battlefield, and recently seized US-supplied military vehicles captured from retreating Saudi-backed forces.
While the Houthis’ stockpile levels are unknown, it is possible to assemble a sense of their firepower and military capabilities.

Wisconsin Palestinian community leader can be deported, immigration judge rules
A US immigration judge ruled on Wednesday that Salah Sarsour, a Muslim and Palestinian community leader in his hometown of Milwaukee, Wisconsin, can be deported per the wishes of the Trump administration.
In a press briefing following the decision, his lawyer, Patrick Taurel, confirmed that he will appeal.
For the time being, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) cannot re-detain Sarsour because a federal judge's order ensuring he walks free remains in place.
As with a number of Palestinian Green Card holders before Sarsour, such as former Columbia University students Mahmoud Khalil and Mohsen Mahdawi, as well as the Georgetown University scholar Badar Khan Suri, who is married to a Palestinian American, the US government arrested Salah in March on the grounds that he is a threat to national security.
His legal team and advocates maintain the arrest was because of his speech in defence of Palestinian rights. Sarsour sits on the board of American Muslims for Palestine (AMP), which pro-Israeli groups have claimed is a front for Hamas.

Saudi Arabia, Yemen call for closer regional ties to counter Houthi attacks
Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman warned on Wednesday that his government will not hesitate to respond decisively to any threat or attack, reaffirming support for the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen to confront the Houthis.
During his annual royal speech at the opening of the Shura Council, he noted that the establishment of the “Mecca Defence Pact” between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan aimed to shield the region from escalating conflict, adding that the kingdom also initiated the establishment of a “multinational defensive maritime coalition” to protect international waterways.
Mohammed bin Salman condemned continued Israeli attacks on the Palestinian territories, as well as the “repeated violations” of the Al-Aqsa Mosque in occupied East Jerusalem, and called for diplomacy to de-escalate conflicts in the region.
Meanwhile, Yemen’s Foreign Minister Afrah Abdulaziz al-Zouba met with the Turkish embassy’s charge d’affaires in Yemen, Amirullah Isler, to discuss regional developments and ways to strengthen ties between “the two brotherly countries”, according to a post shared on X by Yemen’s Foreign Ministry.
The Turkish envoy reaffirmed Ankara’s “steadfast supportive stance” toward the Yemeni government, and Zouba stressed the need for closer political and diplomatic coordination to counter Houthi threats to the Red Sea, the statement added.

Iraq celebrates as last US troops withdraw from country
The US removed its last troops from Iraq on Wednesday, 23 years after Washington invaded the country to topple former Iraqi President Saddam Hussein from power, in an intervention that cost over $1 trillion and led to hundreds of thousands of deaths over the last two decades.
"Today, the United States and our Coalition partners formally concluded Operation Inherent Resolve in Iraq, consistent with the September 2024 US-Iraq joint statement and US national interests," the Pentagon said in a statement.
The US first occupied Iraq in 2003, following the overthrow of Hussein, before pulling out its forces in 2011. They returned at the request of the Iraqi government in 2014 to tackle the spread of the Islamic State (IS) militant group, which had seized around a third of the country.
The US began withdrawing troops from Iraq in 2025, with soldiers relocating from Ain al-Asad base in Anbar Province and the Victory Base Complex, located within the Baghdad International Airport, to Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdish region.
Iraqi Kurdistan was granted some semi-autonomy in 2005. For example, it has its own prime minister, president, and a separate security force, the Peshmerga.

Morocco’s King Mohammed VI has appointed Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri as head of the government, one week after her party won the legislative elections.
For the first time in its history, the North African kingdom will be led by a woman.
“This is truly a historic moment,” El Mansouri told public media after her audience at the royal palace.
“For the first time in our country’s history, a woman is taking on the responsibility of leading the government. This is not only a source of pride for me, but for all Moroccan women,” she added.
At 50, the lawyer becomes the thrid woman in the Arab world to reach this position, after Najla Bouden and Sarra Zaafarani in Tunisia.
El Mansouri had already made history by becoming, at just 33, the first woman to serve as mayor of the tourist city of Marrakesh in 2009 - a position she currently holds for a second term since 2021.
She had also made her mark during the 2023 earthquake, visiting affected communities repeatedly.
Currently the national coordinator of the Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM), outgoing minister of housing and spatial planning, and a newly re-elected MP, El Mansouri had been widely tipped for the role in recent weeks.
However, without an absolute majority, the new prime minister will now need to form a coalition government for the next five years ahead of the 9 October parliamentary session.

A 72-hour-old newborn is laid to sleep on a thin, worn-out mattress on the floor of a school in Sidon, south Lebanon, his first days unfolding in a classroom-turned-shelter.
His mother, Hala Loubany, 29, has just had a C-section. She watches over the baby boy, one hand resting protectively over the throbbing scar on her stomach.
Next to them, separated by a shelf crammed with canned food and clothes, an elderly man is preparing lunch for himself and his wife.
Three families live in this classroom, their few belongings packed into corners as they wait to return to Nabatieh’s southern district.
Israel's bombardment has destroyed infrastructure, including thousands of homes, across south Lebanon, with more than two dozen Lebanese border towns and villages razed. Tens of thousands of people have been displaced.
“Hala’s water broke here, in the school, so she was taken to the hospital at the last minute,” her father, Ali Mahmoud Loubany, told Middle East Eye. “It was an emergency so doctors performed a C-section.”
Hala was six months pregnant when she, her husband, their two sons, aged six and one, and her father fled Nabatieh. The school in Sidon is the second shelter they have been forced to seek refuge in.
Directly opposite the classroom is the only women’s bathroom on the floor. Families have to schedule showers in the three laminate stalls and wash their clothes in the shallow sinks.
For Hala, who is still recovering from surgery, poor sanitation is a major source of anxiety, as she worries about her wound becoming infected.

When Grand Ayatollah Mousa Shobeiri Zanjani died at 98 on 20 September, he left behind a rare position in Iran’s religious establishment: a cleric who kept his distance from political power, yet whose influence reached across the Islamic Republic’s deepest political divides.
His students included former reformist President Mohammad Khatami and, according to a source in the Qom Seminary, Mojtaba Khamenei, the current supreme leader. For decades, politicians and clerics on opposing sides of Iran’s political spectrum turned to Shobeiri because his authority rested outside politics.
That independence made him an important figure at moments when Iran’s political and religious establishments collided.
Shobeiri was one of seven senior clerics identified by the Society of Seminary Scholars of Qom in the 1990s as qualified to be followed as a grand ayatollah and serve as a marja, or religious authority.
The ayatollah belonged to a strand of the Iranian clergy that believed clerics should not directly enter politics.
They are often described as “traditional” clerics, a group that includes Ayatollah Vahid Khorasani, another highly respected figure in the seminary establishment. Both men have largely stayed outside of the Islamic Republic's factional politics.
Traditional clerics tend to see their role primarily as preserving the independence of the seminaries from the state, maintaining the institution of marjaʿiyyah – the system of senior religious authorities whom believers may follow for guidance on matters of Islamic law – and addressing religious and social affairs rather than directly participating in political power.

As the US pulls its forces out of Iraq, what happens to Iran-backed armed groups?
The US has announced the withdrawal of its forces from Iraq, 23 years after the invasion that overthrew Saddam Hussein.
The development has been hailed by the Iraqi government as a final return to "national sovereignty" after years of American involvement in the country.
"October 1 will be a new day in the course of the Iraqi state, with the country free of any foreign military presence and the completion of national sovereignty over its territory," Iraq's Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said in a statement.
His statement is not quite accurate - Turkey still maintains a military presence in the country, though it has also pledged to soon hand over its Bashiqa-Zilkan military base in northern Iraq to the government.
The end of the US presence in Iraq, the deadline for which was 30 September, had originally also been tied to the disarming of the extra-government armed groups that, since the overthrow of Saddam, have been among the most powerful forces in the country.

A crisis involving Turkish investment funds accused of running Ponzi-like schemes has affected half a million people, with authorities ordering the liquidation of some 130 funds worth $17bn earlier this month.
Already historic in scale, the financial turmoil has quickly become a major political crisis for President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s administration, exposing a web of connections between the funds, their managers and the ruling elite.
The most prominent political casualty so far has been Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya, a deputy head of the ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) and family minister from 2016 to 2018. She resigned on Sunday after the opposition accused her of making substantial profits from share sales shortly before the funds crisis triggered a major stock market sell-off on 16 September.
Erdogan addressed the controversy on Monday, pledging to pursue those responsible for market manipulation and fraudulent trading schemes.
“Whoever lays a hand on the nation's rights, assets or legal interests will face us and the state,” he said.
The funds in question concentrated their holdings in illiquid stocks with low free floats, making their prices easier to inflate because relatively few shares were available for trading. For example, the Tera investment fund generated a return of over 1,500 percent over the past year, a figure that is totally illogical by any market calculation or method.

The UAE has officially acknowledged hosting Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for talks with President Mohammed bin Zayed on Sunday, its first such acknowledgement since establishing relations with Israel in 2020.
In a statement late on Monday, the Emirates News Agency said simply that bin Zayed "discussed with the Israeli prime minister the bilateral relations between the two countries and ways to strengthen and develop them".
The UAE released no official photograph of Sunday’s meeting. Its statement made no mention of the regional wars in which the UAE and Israel are involved - in occupied Palestine, Lebanon, Syria, Iran and Sudan.
Sources in the UAE told Haaretz that bin Zayed greeted Netanyahu at the airport.
The meeting also made the front pages of the UAE’s state-owned Al-Bayan and Al-Ittihad newspapers, which simply reprinted the official statement.
In May, Netanyahu’s office blindsided the UAE by revealing that he had secretly visited the country at the height of the Israeli-US war on Iran.
The Emirati foreign ministry responded by saying its relations with Israel "are public" and "not based on non-transparent or unofficial arrangements".
"Any claims regarding unannounced visits or undisclosed arrangements are entirely unfounded unless officially announced by the relevant authorities in the UAE," the statement said.
'Moral support'
